title: Asthma Exacerbations Following Wildfire Smoke PM2.5 Exposure Among U.S. Adults
content:
Abstract

Asthma exacerbation can be triggered by various forms of air pollution, including PM2.5 from wildfire smoke. This study aims to investigate the association between wildfire smoke PM2.5 exposure and asthma exacerbations in adults during the warm months (April–August) between 2006 and 2019. Using a case-crossover design, we analyzed 18,935 asthma exacerbation events and four matched control periods per event from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) All of Us research program. We used the conditional logistic regression to estimate the association (odds ratios [ORs]) between wildfire smoke PM2.5 exposure and asthma exacerbation, considering lag periods of 0–7 days and adjusting for temperature, precipitation, and humidity. Significant positive associations were observed across all lag periods, with adjusted ORs ranging from 1.27 (95% CI: 1.22–1.33) to 1.38 (95% CI: 1.32–1.44). Stratified analyses showed higher odds of asthma exacerbation among older adults, non-Hispanic Whites, midwestern residents, and those exposed in May. These findings highlight the potential contribution of wildfire smoke PM2.5 to asthma exacerbations in adults and the importance of targeted public health strategies to reduce exposure during wildfire events.
